Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns

Coordinate specialized agents with delegation, shared state, or cross-critique—supported by typed messages, bounded calls, and explicit failure handling.

Explore the slides

Choose coordination around the task

The deck starts with the limits of a single agent carrying many overlapping tools and a large prompt. It then introduces three ways to coordinate narrower agents, each with a different trade-off in control, flexibility, and cost.

Multi-agent orchestration patterns compared
PatternCoordinationBest fitWatch for
Supervisor-workerDecompose, delegate, synthesizeClear subtasks with distinct skillsCentral routing bottlenecks
BlackboardRead and update shared stateExploration with evolving next stepsConflicting or overwritten updates
Debate and consensusIndependent answers, critique, adjudicationAmbiguous questions requiring comparisonExtra calls, token cost, and inconclusive rounds

Messaging and resilience support every pattern

Make communication traceable

A typed message envelope identifies sender, receiver, message type, payload, and correlation ID. Correlation IDs connect requests and responses across asynchronous steps. Deadline or time-to-live handling must be enforced by the runtime to bound waiting.

Contain partial failures

Use per-call timeouts and an overall workflow budget. A circuit breaker tracks repeated failures, pauses calls during a cooldown, and selects an explicit fallback. A fallback may be a simpler agent, a cached result, or escalation to a person.

Keep workflows bounded and observable

  • Test specialized workers independently.
  • Track shared-state changes when debugging blackboard workflows.
  • Cap debate rounds and compare their benefit with added cost.
  • Record failed calls and fallback outcomes rather than silently dropping work.

The original slides include illustrative code and token-cost estimates. These examples explain design patterns; they are not complete production implementations or universal performance guarantees.

Slide 2: Why Single-Agent Systems Break Down

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
THE PROBLEM 00 ANTI-PATTERN Why Single-Agent Systems Break Down TOOLS = [search_web, run_sql, send_email, call_payment_api, parse_pdf, write_code, query_crm, ...] # 40+ agent = Agent( model="gpt-4", tools=TOOLS, # grows every release system_prompt=MEGA_PROMPT, # 3,000+ tokens ) response = agent.run(user_request) # Confuses near-duplicate tools, picks the # wrong one, burns context before the model # even starts reasoning about the task SYMPTOMS ✦ Tool confusion: overlapping tools (send_email vs. notify_slack) get picked almost at random ✦ Context bloat: every tool schema plus the mega-prompt eats budget before reasoning starts ✦ No separation of concerns: one prompt tweak risks every capability at once ✦ Opaque debugging: a single giant trace hides which "skill" actually failed ✦ Fix: split into narrow, specialized agents coordinated by an orchestration pattern

Slide 3: Supervisor-Worker: Hierarchical Delegation

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
PATTERN 01 01 SUPERVISOR-WORKER Hierarchical Delegation class Supervisor: def __init__(self, workers): self.workers = workers self.router = Agent(model= "gpt-4") def handle(self, task): plan = self.router.run( f "Split into subtasks, assign one " f "of {list(self.workers)}: {task}" ) results = [ self.workers[s.agent].run(s.step) for s in plan.subtasks ] return self.router.run( f "Synthesize final answer: {results}" ) WHY IT WORKS ✦ The router owns decomposition and delegation only — it holds no domain tools of its own ✦ Workers stay narrow: 3-5 tools each, a focused system prompt, independently testable ✦ A synthesis step lets the supervisor reconcile conflicting worker outputs ✦ Scales horizontally — add a new worker type without touching existing ones ✦ Watch for: the supervisor becoming a serial bottleneck if every step routes through it

Slide 4: Blackboard: Shared-State Collaboration

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
PATTERN 02 02 BLACKBOARD Shared-State Collaboration class Blackboard: def __init__(self): self.state = {"facts": [], "open_qs": [], "draft": None} def post(self, update): self.state["facts"] += update["facts"] self.state["open_qs"] = update["open_qs"] if update.get("draft"): self.state["draft"] = update["draft"] def run(board, agents, max_rounds= 5): for _ in range(max_rounds): if not board.state[ "open_qs"]: return board.state[ "draft"] for agent in agents: board.post(agent.run(board.state)) return board.state[ "draft"] WHY IT WORKS ✦ No fixed call order — any agent can read or write shared state each round ✦ Fits exploratory tasks where the next useful step depends on what was just found ✦ The loop ends when open_qs empties, not after a fixed number of steps ✦ Risk: agents overwriting each other's updates — namespace or version each write ✦ Trace the whole blackboard state per round, not just one agent's output, when debugging

Slide 5: Debate and Consensus

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
PATTERN 03 03 DEBATE & CONSENSUS Cross-Critique for High-Stakes Calls def debate(question, agent_a, agent_b, rounds= 2): pos_a = agent_a.run(f "Answer: {question}" ) pos_b = agent_b.run(f "Answer: {question}" ) for _ in range(rounds): new_a = agent_a.run( f "Critique and revise vs: {pos_b}" ) new_b = agent_b.run( f "Critique and revise vs: {pos_a}" ) pos_a, pos_b = new_a, new_b judge = Agent(model= "gpt-4") return judge.run( f"Pick the stronger answer:\n" f"A: {pos_a}\nB: {pos_b}" ) WHY IT WORKS ✦ Independent first answers avoid anchoring on whichever agent spoke first ✦ Cross-critique surfaces errors neither agent catches reasoning alone ✦ A separate judge (or a vote across 3+ agents) breaks ties without favoring A ✦ Costs 4-6x the tokens of a single call — reserve for genuinely ambiguous decisions ✦ Cap rounds at 2-3: debates converge quickly or not at all after that

Slide 6: Typed Agent Messaging

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
INFRASTRUCTURE 04 AGENT MESSAGING A Typed Protocol Between Agents @dataclass class AgentMessage: sender: str receiver: str type: Literal["request", "response", "error", "event"] payload: dict correlation_id: str ttl_s: int = 30 class MessageRouter: def __init__(self): self.inboxes = defaultdict( list) def send(self, msg): if msg.type == "request" and msg.ttl_s <= 0: raise TimeoutError(msg.correlation_id) self.inboxes[msg.receiver].append(msg) WHY IT WORKS ✦ A typed envelope — not raw strings — lets you log, replay, and version agent traffic ✦ correlation_id ties a request to its response across async hops, which tracing needs ✦ type discriminates request/response/error/event so routers never guess payload shape ✦ ttl_s bounds how long a pending request can block a waiting caller ✦ This is the same shape emerging A2A and MCP-adjacent protocols are standardizing on

Slide 7: Partial Failures and Circuit Breakers

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
RESILIENCE 05 PARTIAL FAILURES Circuit Breakers Between Agents class AgentCircuitBreaker: def __init__(self, agent, fallback, limit= 3, cool=60): self.agent, self.fallback = agent, fallback self.limit, self.cool = limit, cool self.fails, self.opened = 0, None def call(self, task): gap = self.opened and time.time() - self.opened if gap and gap < self.cool: return self.fallback.run(task) try: out = self.agent.run(task, timeout= 15) self.fails = 0 return out except (TimeoutError, AgentError): self.fails += 1 if self.fails >= self.limit: self.opened = time.time() return self.fallback.run(task) WHY IT WORKS ✦ One slow or failing worker should never hang the whole multi-agent pipeline ✦ The breaker trips after repeated failures and routes to a cheaper fallback agent ✦ A cooldown window stops hammering a worker that's only temporarily degraded ✦ Always set per-call timeouts — an orchestrator with no budget runs forever ✦ Fallback can be a simpler model, a cached answer, or "escalate to a human" — never a silent drop

Slide 8: Choosing an Orchestration Pattern

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
DECISION GUIDE Choosing an Orchestration Pattern Supervisor-Worker Router decomposes a task and delegates to narrow, specialized workers, then synthesizes. Blackboard Agents read/write shared state in any order until open questions resolve. Debate & Consensus Independent answers, cross-critique over rounds, resolved by a judge or vote. Messaging + Resilience Typed envelopes, correlation IDs, timeouts and circuit breakers across agents. PATTERN BEST FOR COMPLEXITY WATCH OUT FOR Supervisor-Worker Clear subtasks with known, distinct skills Medium Router becomes a serial bottleneck Blackboard Exploratory work where step order isn't known upfront Med-High Agents overwrite each other's state Debate & Consensus High-stakes or ambiguous, single-answer decisions High (tokens) 4-6x token cost; cap rounds at 2-3 Messaging + Breaker Any multi-agent system crossing process boundaries Low to build No timeout budget = pipeline hangs ! Pro tip: Start with Supervisor-Worker for most multi-agent tasks — reach for Blackboard or Debate only when task order is genuinely unknown or the stakes justify the extra token cost.

Frequently asked questions

What is multi-agent orchestration?

Multi-agent orchestration coordinates specialized agents, their tasks, shared information, messages, and failures to produce an overall result.

When does supervisor-worker orchestration fit?

It fits tasks with clear subtasks and distinct skills. A supervisor decomposes the request, delegates work, and synthesizes results. Its central routing role can become a bottleneck.

How does a blackboard pattern work?

Agents contribute to shared state containing facts, open questions, or drafts. The workflow evolves as information arrives. Namespaced or versioned updates help prevent conflicting writes.

What is debate-based consensus?

Agents produce independent initial answers, critique alternatives, and revise their positions. A judge or vote resolves the final result. Additional calls increase cost, so the workflow needs a round limit.

What belongs in an agent message?

The deck uses sender, receiver, message type, payload, correlation ID, and a time-to-live field. These support routing, tracing, and bounded requests when enforced by the runtime.

How should an orchestrator handle worker failures?

Set per-call timeouts and an overall budget. Circuit breakers can stop repeated calls to a failing worker and route to an explicit fallback, such as a simpler model, cached response, or human escalation.
